title: Satire is a vital tool for challenging power, and it's being undermined
subtitle: Political comedy has lost its sting
author: Richard P. Martin
introduction: Comedy and satire are widely seen as forms of entertainment, but they remain vital tools for challenging power. Yet in today’s media landscape, dominated by fleeting stand-up routines and viral clips, mockery is easily absorbed, ignored, or contained by those it targets. Stanford Professor Richard P. Martin argues that this has stripped satire of its political force. While figures like Jimmy Kimmel show its continued relevance, real impact requires a return to more public, theatrical, and sustained forms of comedy.
body:
Total moron. Short-fingered vulgarian. Fat orange fascist. The problem is, even the best jeers are satisfying in the moment but ultimately inefficacious. As schoolyard doctrine has long held, it is sticks and stones that really break bones. Yet adults (mostly) don’t feel good hurling rocks instead of insults (quite rightly). So that’s the frustration—how do we make mockery get results?

Real bullets bounce off Godzilla; forget about the verbal equivalent. People cling to the comforting belief that stand-up comedians, whether late-night TV hosts or gritty open-mic aspirants, are speaking truth to power. Nice idea, but naïve. Stand-up—the default medium for modern mockery—doesn’t cut it. Short blasts, however witty or venomous, dissipate like short-term memories. What is more, the potential threat from voices crying in the desert can easily be co-opted or ignored, as has recently been demonstrated by authorities in the US and Saudi Arabia.

What Kimmel’s reinstatement showed was just how irrelevant his excellent criticisms of POTUS had all been over the long run.

First: closer to (my) home. Jimmy Kimmel, the brilliant late-night comedian on ABC, had the temerity in September 2025 to point out that a recently murdered young activist, Charlie Kirk, was perhaps not material for canonization, despite fervent efforts by right-wingers to sanctify him. Immediately, conservative ire ignited. One of those who claimed to appreciate the late Kirk was the president of the US (hereafter “POTUS”—has no one yet realized that the Latin adjective meaning “drunk” is an odd acronym for a famous teetotaler?). Stung for years by Kimmel’s nightly barbs, this time POTUS backed his handpicked head of the Federal Communications Commission in threats to derail a merger deal involving the parent company of ABC (Walt Disney Co.). Within 48 hours of his original MAGA-infuriating monologue, Kimmel was off the air.

To its credit, a non-trivial slice of America—the place that one recent commentator aptly described as, “A nation of anxious primates trapped in a silicon casino of likes, retweets, and dopamine-soaked drudgery”—woke up long enough to protest the POTUS-sanctioned suspension, with lines of demonstrators snaking around Disney headquarters in Los Angeles and New York. Some suits in the C-suite had second thoughts, in which the phrase “advertising revenue” no doubt featured prominently, and within a week Kimmel was back, gracefully unapologetic. Surely a win for democracy, for free speech, for comedy!

To the contrary: what Kimmel’s reinstatement showed was just how irrelevant his excellent criticisms of POTUS (and FLOTUS and SCOTUS, to boot) had all been over the long run. Supporters tuned them out (or more likely never watched the show); the opposition imbibed them and felt good. But be assured: if Kimmel had really possessed the key to civic destabilization that some attributed to him, his show would long ago have been deep-sixed.

How do you mock, belittle, abuse, and deflate the monsters (given that they will never feel shame)? One answer is to leverage the brain and get dramatic.

The Saudi example at first seems a world away but comes down to the same reflex—swallowing some scattershot standup shtick in order to dodge really dangerous satirical critique. Two weeks after the Kimmel incident, thousands attended the first-ever Riyadh Comedy Festival, part of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s push to paint a kinder gentler face on his kingdom. A number of Western comedians turned down invitations to perform, but dozens more took the bait, reportedly banking anywhere from $300,000 to $1.6 million USD. To the astonishment of some observers, they joked on the big Boulevard City stage about things like trans persons, the niqab, and women driving—edgy material, it might seem, given the environs.

Hardly mentioned, however, were the ground rules that had allowed the show to go on, prohibiting “any material considered to degrade, defame, or bring into public disrepute, contempt, scandal, embarrassment, or ridicule” the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, including jokes about the royal family or religion. Most conspicuously, comedians ignored the Human Rights Watch scholar Joey Shea, who advised beforehand, “Everyone performing in Riyadh should use this high-profile opportunity to call for the release of detained Saudi activists,” while observing that the festival overlapped with the seventh anniversary of journalist Jamal Khashoggi’s murder.

Cutting through the hype around both events, one realizes how power really deals with the annoying buzz of stand-up. One-liners can’t bite through a corporate carapace; spray enough apparent tolerance around and the haze may even make politicians look benign. What’s the alternative? How do you mock, belittle, abuse, and deflate the monsters (given that they will never feel shame)? One answer is to leverage the brain and get dramatic. Psychologists and neuroscientists have shown that emotional memories, processed by the amygdala, last much longer, and get stored deeper down, as it were, than episodic memories that are handled by the hippocampus. Live drama, with its immediacy, suspense, and close audience involvement, makes for an ideal creator of strong emotion, and thus for lasting impressions. Jokes you forget, but good plays you can’t help but re-play in the mind. Good funny plays, even better.

We happen to have a superb model for constructing precisely the sort of brain-penetrating art that's needed right now: Aristophanes. That is to say, bring back full-scale, two-hour-long bawdy comedic fantasies, brimming with memorable creative obscenities and wild rants, demeaning plots, dehumanizing tropes, crazy props, and some catchy music and dance routines. Direct such concoctions toward a (lightly fictionized) target in order to publicly and totally devastate his/her image. Scapegoat the powerful (not coincidentally, ancient Athenians also invented annual political ostracisms). Does your dictator dream of being a drama queen? Make him the centerpiece of his very own play. Shove it into the long-term memory of the viewing public. Then laugh him out of town.

Aristophanes, whose career spanned the last quarter of the 5th century BC and the first decades of the 4th, is most famous today for two productions of the 44 or so he is known to have put on stage in the Theater of Dionysos, a vital institutional site of democratic Athens, occupying the south slope of the Acropolis. The comic drama Lysistrata (411 BC) enacted a double-pronged plan to coerce Athenian men into ending the disastrous Peloponnesian War. A gang of feisty older women invades the Acropolis to block access to its central bank. Meanwhile, younger women, led by “She who Dissolves Armies” (Lusi-strata) carry out their oath to refuse sex to their men until combat ceases. Predictably (after some frustrated hard-on scenes) peace soon ensues. (True, the Lysistrata Project, involving 1000 readings of this play in 59 countries, did not stop the 2003 invasion of Iraq, but it did intensify criticism of Bush and Blair.)

The second most famous Aristophanic romp, the Clouds (423 BC), satirized Socrates the philosopher by cunningly (if not maliciously) distorting his teachings. Instead of guiding people to examine their lives, with injunctions about knowing the limits of their supposed wisdom, Aristophanes’ “Socrates” experiments with the physiology of gnat-farts and flea-jumps; explores the heavens in an elevated basket; finds rhetorical tricks to make the weaker argument appear to be the stronger; and dismisses the traditional gods in favor of cosmic forces like The Whirl. When a desperate hick enrolls his son in The Thinkery so he can acquire the latest sophistic argument to bail his dad out of debt, the young man ends up learning from the amoral casuist “Socrates” that, among other things, parricide is not so horrible. The enraged tuition-paying father burns down Socrates’ school (apparently, with sage and staff still inside).

This show made the leap into long-term Athenian memory, if Plato’s later Apology of his teacher Socrates is any indication. In this speech of 399 BC, defending himself against the charge of “corrupting the youth,” the real Socrates is quoted as blaming the comedian (Plato Apology 19c) for having depicted him as a criminally irreligious, nutty professor, thereby prejudicing the jury against him (albeit nearly a quarter-century after the play’s production date).

It’s highly unlikely Aristophanes ever intended to rid Athens of Socrates. The two are in fact depicted as drinking partners in another Platonic dialogue, the Symposium, set seven years after the comedy debuted. That’s where the playwright makes a glorious mythopoeic speech (the study of which is now officially banned in some Texas universities) sketching the origins of same-sex love. Besides, the Clouds actually had come in dead-last in the competition at the Dionysia festival of 423 BC—hardly an immediate hit. Yet Aristophanes’ brilliant satire rippled far beyond its single performance on stage that early Spring day, with real-world effects one would find hard to envision now.

Grab the headlines and name real names, represented by tangibly real bodies on stage.

Of course, nobody wants a comic production to end with a celebrity forced to drink hemlock (as Socrates finally did). That’s why the neo-Aristophanic cure that I’m prescribing for contemporary comic dropsy should instead take as its model a lesser-known play about civic rot that is uncannily prescient: the Knights, produced in 424 BC. This play was most likely spun off from the Babylonians (426 BC, now surviving via a few fragments) in which Aristophanes mercilessly pummeled his nemesis Cleon, a demagogue who had gained power in Athens after the death of the statesman Pericles.

To the historian and general Thucydides, Cleon was a bloodthirsty thug: when Mytilene on the island of Lesbos revolted against its imperial master Athens in 427 BC, it was Cleon who introduced the proposal to put to death all its male citizens, and to enslave the women and children. As the historian records, only a last-minute reconsideration in the Assembly the next day spared the city.

Aristophanes came to clash with Cleon over the latter’s charge that the playwright belittled Athens (and Cleon’s state policies) in his comedy Babylonians and, what was worse, did so in the presence of many foreign visitors who had come to the popular Spring festival dedicated to Dionysus.  Aristophanes beat the rap and then wrote about it in his play Acharnians (425 BC): “He hauled me before the Council, and slandered me, and tongue-lashed me with lies, and roared like the Cycloborus [a loud local river], and soaked me in abuse, so that I nearly died in a mephitic miasma of misadventure” (as Jeffrey Henderson translates in his Loeb Classical Library edition). In the Knights the next year, the bull-roaring Cleon appears very lightly disguised as “Paphlagon,” household steward to the doddering old man “Dêmos” (or “the people,” as in dêmo-kratia—i.e. Athens itself). Always screaming, taking bribes from domestic slaves on the promise that he won’t beat them, extorting merchants, squeezing money out of the magistrates, Cleon/Paphlagon neatly embodies the ultimate sleazy politician. In a race to the bottom to outdo the Sausage-Seller (an upstart rival for the stewardship), Paphlagon resorts to increasingly desperate toadying toward the apparently senile Dêmos (“Please sir, wipe your nose on my head!”).

SUGGESTED READING Absurdity confronts the fragility of power By Kirk Ormand

The turning point of the comedy comes in a frantic farcical scene based on food (which, in Aristophanes, just edges out sex as a focal point): Sausage-Seller and Paphlagon try to outdo one another in stuffing Dêmos with delicacies. Only when it is revealed that the former is earnestly giving his all, while Paphlagon has been hoarding fish fillets, tasty paunches, and cheesecake for himself, does Dêmos kick him out. Showing that he has been onto the bully’s scummy tricks all along, Dêmos is then magically rejuvenated, sleek and gleaming like the vigorous Athens of its glory days. All ends happily.

So, taking a page from the Knights, here are a half-dozen production notes for the critically needed Aristophanes of 2026—wherever you might be:

  1. Target the contemporary. Sure, we have a few political musical comedies—but Hamilton doesn’t exactly beat down bad guys. South Park is suitably offensive—but it’s a cartoon, and wonderful as they are, animated characters don’t offer the same convincing emotional immediacy as living, breathing people like us on a stage. Grab the headlines and name real names, represented by tangibly real bodies on stage. Take as a guide what the Chorus in the Knights asserts:

λοιδορῆσαι τοὺς πονηροὺς οὐδέν ἐστ᾿ ἐπίφθονον,

ἀλλὰ τιμὴ τοῖσι χρηστοῖς, ὅστις εὖ λογίζεται.

There’s nothing invidious about calling bad people names;

it’s a way to honor good people, if you stop to think about it.

  1. Work in as many raw and insulting jibes as you can. Aristophanes’ range from the mild (“garlic breath”) to the extra-spicy (“having a capacious anus,” “licking women’s honeypots”). And don't stick with simple epithets—paint the picture, as in one of the many descriptors of Paphlagon’s extortions: “He’s got his legs spread so far apart that his arsehole’s smack dab over Buggerland, his hand’s in Shake Downs, and his mind’s on Crime-a.”

  2. Wild plots and dream-like imagery trump mere shit-posting; vivid visible material makes drama memorable. Why just talk about peace treaties when you can embody them as vintages of desirable wine, or stage Peace herself as a voluptuous woman, or turn foggy sophistic notions into a chorus of Clouds? Come up with over-the-top emojis and then make them do things (“drama” means “doing” after all) in the service of full-blown mûthoi (Aristotle’s term for plots, the “myths” that capture a narrative arc).

  3. Give them music, dance, pratfalls—and blur the boundaries between real and imaginary. Aristophanic plays contained an intermezzo section (the “parabasis” or “stepping aside”) in which the chorus or its leader took on the persona of the real comic writer and talked about current events from his point of view, while still masked and costumed as their dramatic selves (old men, farmers, women at a ritual, etc.). It’s not really “him” who is insulting and lampooning the powers-that-be then; it’s just a song-and-dance, right? Prosecuting an offender gets conveniently harder.

  4. It takes a village: put a chorus on stage, a metonymic chunk of the people whom you are addressing. Have it consist of real people with a stake in the action. In Knights, it was 24 men enacting an elite military corps who became fed up with Cleon’s political adventurism. The choruses in Athenian drama and music festivals were comprised of friends and neighbors of the audience, not professionals: the whole crowd (anywhere from 5000 to 10,000 spectators) would be rooting for them as well as for their play, which meant that comic competitions resembled a football match. Along these lines, imagine an anti-ICE comedy, taking on the notorious Immigration and Customs Enforcement with a chorus of the undocumented. Our word “comedy” comes from the Greek for a kind of “community,” used at least as early as the 6th century BC. It’s the product either of “singers at a kômos”—a late-night unruly procession of revelers—or of “singers from the kômê”—a village (probably with decidedly anti-establishment opinions).

  5. Upload and spread it. When you come down to it, libel laws and nervous producers are what combine to keep really incisive contemporary political satire off the stage in the UK and US. Enter the internet, the most potentially powerful comic community. Let the fun begin*.*
